title: continuous batching scheduler - token-level vs request-level (draft)
content:
Status: draft
Author: Sofia Martinez (eng-serving-runtime)
Summary:
This draft examines designs for the continuous batching scheduler used in the Redwood serving runtime, focusing on the tradeoffs between token-level and request-level batching, fairness models, and interactions with the KV-cache and kernel execution. The goal is a pragmatic design that maximizes GPU utilization and throughput while meeting per-request latency SLOs and providing predictable fairness across tenants and priorities.

Goals and constraints:
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 200ms for interactive routes; p99 targets depend on tier.
- Maximize GPU token throughput (tokens/sec) and kernel occupancy.
- Avoid head-of-line blocking that causes long tails for short requests.
- Support multi-tenant fairness and per-route priorities (paid vs free).
- Keep implementation complexity manageable for a first iteration.

Background:
We currently bundle requests into batches before kernel invocation. Two main batching granularities are under consideration:
1) Request-level batching: group complete requests (multiple tokens) that are ready to execute at kernel time. Batching unit is a request.
2) Token-level batching (continuous batching): schedule at the token timestep, pulling partial progress from many requests and executing a single token-step kernel across the batch.

High-level pros/cons:
- Request-level batching:
  - Simpler to implement (existing code paths).
  - Easier to maintain per-request bookkeeping (no interrupt/resume).
  - Batching efficiency depends on request arrival alignment; long requests can dominate batch slots.
  - May underutilize kernels for long-sequence models with variable lengths.

- Token-level batching:
  - Higher utilization for streaming/interactive workloads: coalesces tokens across requests at each step.
  - Better latency for short requests because they can be interleaved with long-running ones rather than waiting for entire-request batching boundaries.
  - More complex: requires preemption, per-request state machine, careful KV cache handling, and micro-batch scheduling.

Fairness considerations:
- Goals: avoid starvation, bound latency amplification, and provide weighted shares for tenants/routes.
- Candidate fairness policies:
  1) Weighted Fair Queueing (WFQ) across routes/tenants.
  2) Shortest-Remaining-Processing-Time (SRPT) bias for low-latency interactive requests (fast-path).
  3) Age-based priority uplift to prevent starvation.
  4) Token-budget per tenant per scheduling window.

Practical hybrid approach (recommended):
- Maintain per-tenant/route lanes with a small number of priority bands: fast-interactive, standard, background.
- Each lane has a token budget and a short time-slice budget used by the token-level scheduler.
- Within each time slice, schedule token-steps from queued requests in a round-robin or deficit-based manner so that short requests progress quickly.
- Interleave SRPT for requests under a short-length threshold to keep tails low for tiny responses.
- Apply age-based uplift if a request waits > X ms (configurable) to prevent starvation.

Token-level implementation details:
- Micro-batch window: a small configurable window (e.g., 2-8ms) where the scheduler collects ready tokens before issuing a kernel call. This balances batching gains vs added scheduling latency.
- Scheduling loop:
  1) On arrival, a request registers and gets assigned to a lane.
  2) When a request becomes ready to produce next token, it enqueues a token-ready event.
  3) Scheduler wakes periodically (micro-batch window) or when a threshold of tokens is reached.
  4) Build batch by selecting tokens from lanes according to fairness policy and token budgets.
  5) Assemble input tensors (pad/truncate per-token context as needed), call kernel, apply outputs, update per-request KV cache pointer and sequence state.
  6) If a request finished, mark completion and record latency.

KV-cache & kernel considerations:
- KV cache locality: continuous batching will interleave cache lookups/updates for many requests. To avoid frequent memory thrashing and copying, we should: 
  - Allocate per-GPU, per-lane cache pools with pre-allocated slab sizes for typical sequence lengths.
  - Use pointer-based referencing to avoid copying KV segments when possible (view/slice semantics).
  - Coalesce GPU memory writes from multiple requests into fewer CUDA calls.
- Kernel alignment: many GPU kernels are optimized for specific batch sizes and token lengths. The scheduler should prefer batch shapes that map well to high-throughput kernels. Heuristics: prefer power-of-two batch sizes or known-good sizes for the model family; maintain an empirical perf table per kernel/model.

Backpressure and admission control:
- Admit new requests up to a global token-in-flight soft limit. If limit is reached, expose backpressure error or queue in a separate admission queue for background lanes.
- For token-level scheduling, track in-flight tokens per tenant and allow burst credits to smooth short bursts.

Preemption and consistency:
- Preemption in token-level scheduling means a request's execution stalls between token steps but must keep KV-cache and decoder state consistent. On preemption: 
  - Persist minimal state in GPU accessible structures (or fast pinned CPU memory if eviction needed).
  - Ensure the resumed token step uses the same KV-cache snapshot and attention offsets.

Observability and SLOs:
- Expose metrics: tokens/sec, batches/sec, batch occupancy, per-lane token wait time, per-request latency breakdown (queueing vs compute vs kvcopy).
- Traces should include per-token scheduling events (enqueue, assigned, kernel start/end).
- Build automatic alerts for fairness violations (e.g., tenant wait > 5x expected) and spike in p99 latency after deployment of scheduler changes.

Benchmark plan:
- Microbenchmarks: single-GPU throughput across synthetic traffic with varied sequence-length distributions (short-only, long-only, mixed). Measure tokens/sec and p95/p99 latency.
- Multi-tenant benchmarks: tenants with skewed weights and mixed priorities to validate fairness budgets.
- KV-stress tests: high-concurrency small requests to ensure KV allocation strategy doesn't thrash GPU memory.
- Kernel sensitivity tests: verify performance for common batch shapes and build perf table.

Risks and TODOs:
- Complexity: token-level scheduler significantly increases code complexity and state management. Keep initial rollout behind a feature flag and limited to specific model families.
- Memory fragmentation: per-request KV-slices can cause fragmentation; need allocator strategy.
- Determinism and debugging: interleaving can make reproducing failures harder. Ensure detailed tracing and deterministic replay harness.
- TODO: prototype a lightweight token-level scheduler in dev cluster and compare to tuned request-level batching for 3 representative models (gpt-medium, llama-2-13b, redwood-curie).
- TODO: finalize fairness parameters and default budgets; run offline simulation using historical traffic traces (GH: redwood/traffic-sim#12).

Open questions for review:
- What is the right micro-batch window for our latency SLOs across regions? (tradeoff: 2ms vs 8ms)
- Should we favor kernel-friendly batch sizes even if that occasionally delays a few tokens (favor throughput over strict latency)?
- How to expose tenant-level quotas vs route-level SLAs in a clean UX for customers?

Appendix: quick decision proposals
- Phase 1 (MVP): Enhanced request-level batching with a per-route short-request fast-path. Implement minimal token-coalescing (coalesce ready tokens across requests when present) without full preemption. Deploy behind FF.
- Phase 2: Full token-level continuous scheduler for interactive routes where mixed-length sequences are common. Provide per-tenant lanes and token budgets.
- Phase 3: Kernel-aware shaping + auto-tuning that adapts micro-batch window and preferred batch sizes per model and hardware.

Notes to reviewers:
- Please focus feedback on the fairness model and operational complexity of token bookkeeping.
- Flag any missing observability signals you need to debug scheduling issues.
- If you have perf logs from prior experiments (Nov 2024

2025) that show token-level wins, paste links in the linked_artifacts list.

End of draft.
